subtype: Absorbing the crowd's excitement or fear [Actor]
passage:
Friday: Rajni rolled her eyes when her cousin Vishal begged her to come to the district kabaddi final. 'It's just boys grabbing legs,' she said. She agreed only because Bua was making samosas for the trip.
Saturday: by the second half Rajni was on her feet on the bench, hoarse, clapping with a hundred strangers. When their team's raider slipped free, she hugged the aunty next to her whom she had never seen before. Then the crowd began a rude chant at the other team's raider, and Rajni was shouting it too, fists up. She didn't even know his name.
Sunday: at breakfast Vishal played a video. Rajni watched herself, red-faced, yelling that chant. 'That wasn't me,' she said. 'Sort of was,' Vishal grinned. She laughed but felt a small twist inside. The hug she was glad about. The chant, she wasn't sure she liked.

qa.q: Why did Rajni agree to go to the kabaddi final?
qa.a: She agreed only because Bua was making samosas for the trip.

qa.q: How did Rajni feel watching the video on Sunday?
qa.a: She was embarrassed and uneasy about the chant, feeling a small twist inside, though she was still glad about the hug.

qa.q: What could Rajni do next time a crowd starts a chant she wouldn't normally say?
qa.a: She could notice the moment, stop and ask herself whether she means it, and keep cheering for her team without joining the insults.

qa.q: How might the other team's raider have experienced that chant?
qa.a: To the raider, a hundred people yelling rude words at him may have felt hostile and hurtful, even though most of them didn't know him.

grounding: A teenage girl who didn't care about kabaddi is swept up by a crowd's joy and anger, hugging a stranger and joining a rude chant she later feels unsure about.

subtype: Absorbing the crowd's excitement or fear [Actor]
passage: Shreya, you're going to your first big concert on Saturday, so let your old music teacher tell you something. My name is Nazia, and in 1986 I was a fifteen-year-old girl at a college fest in Hyderabad. Some band from Shillong was playing. I didn't even know their songs. But when three thousand people jumped, I jumped. I climbed onto a chair and sang words I was inventing. I cried at a slow song I'd never heard before. It was the happiest night, and honestly, half that happiness came from the people around me. Then, at the end, somebody at the gate shouted and the crowd surged, and the fear arrived just as fast. I pushed the girl in front of me. I never push anyone. So enjoy it, Shreya. Let the joy in. Just keep a little corner of yourself that notices which feelings are yours.

qa.q: Where was Nazia in 1986?
qa.a: She was a fifteen-year-old girl at a college fest in Hyderabad.

qa.q: What does Nazia mean by 'half that happiness came from the people around me'?
qa.a: She felt a joy that wasn't only hers; the crowd's excitement filled her even for songs she didn't know.

qa.q: What could Shreya do at the concert if the crowd suddenly surges?
qa.a: Shreya could use that little corner of Shreya's own mind to notice the fear rising, keep some space and avoid pushing, and move out calmly.

qa.q: How might the girl in front of Nazia have felt when she was pushed?
qa.a: She probably felt scared and shaken, caught in a crush where even people who never push were pushing.

grounding: A teacher tells a student how, at fifteen, a concert crowd filled her with joy and then fear that weren't wholly her own and made her act unusually.

subtype: Absorbing the crowd's excitement or fear [Actor]
passage: Rain stopped the one-day match at the Guwahati stadium after only twelve overs, and for two hours Sabina and her cousin Bhupen sat under their plastic sheet in the stands. The crowd grew restless. Someone started booing the ground staff. The boo spread along the row, then the whole stand. Sabina, who normally apologises to waiters, found herself on her feet, booing and shouting that the umpires were cheats. When a man two rows down threw a water bottle onto the field, she lifted her own empty cup to throw. Bhupen caught her wrist. 'Sabina. What are you doing?' She looked at the cup in her hand as if it belonged to someone else. Her face was burning. She sat down, her heart still pounding with an anger that didn't feel like hers. The covers stayed on until the match was abandoned.

qa.q: What did the man two rows down throw onto the field?
qa.a: He threw a water bottle onto the field.

qa.q: What does Sabina looking at the cup 'as if it belonged to someone else' suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she was shocked at herself; the anger had come from the crowd and pulled her into something she wouldn't normally do.

qa.q: What helped Sabina stop at the key moment?
qa.a: Bhupen caught her wrist and said her name, which broke the spell long enough for her to see what she was doing and sit down.

qa.q: How might the ground staff have felt during the booing?
qa.a: The ground staff were only doing their job in the rain, so being booed by a whole stand may have felt unfair and frightening.

grounding: A teenage girl kept waiting by rain is swept into a crowd's anger, booing and nearly throwing a cup, until her cousin stops her and she feels it wasn't her own feeling.

subtype: Absorbing the crowd's excitement or fear [Actor]
passage: Sonali had come to the Kolkata football derby only because Darshan had a spare ticket. She didn't know a single player's name. But when sixty thousand people rose for the first attack, she rose too. By half-time she was shouting a chant she'd learnt ten minutes earlier, arms around strangers. When the referee waved off a goal, a roar of anger rolled down the stand, and Sonali found herself yelling at a man in black she could barely see, fists up, face hot. Darshan stared at her. "You?" In the ninety-first minute they scored, and she hugged an uncle she'd never met. On the metro home, voice gone, she felt oddly empty and oddly happy. "I don't even like football," she croaked. "Tonight you did," said Darshan.

qa.q: Why had Sonali come to the derby?
qa.a: Only because Darshan had a spare ticket.

qa.q: How did Sonali feel on the metro home, and what does it suggest?
qa.a: She felt oddly empty and oddly happy, suggesting the huge feelings had come partly from the crowd and drained away once she left it.

qa.q: When the anger rolled down the stand, what could Sonali have done to stay in charge of herself?
qa.a: She could notice that the fury was more the crowd's than her own, lower her fists and take a breath, while still enjoying the shared joy.

qa.q: How did Sonali's yelling look to Darshan?
qa.a: Darshan was astonished, since the Sonali he knew didn't even follow football, which is why he stared and said "You?"

grounding: A teenager at her first football derby is swept up in the crowd's joy and anger, and acts unlike her usual self.

subtype: Absorbing the crowd's excitement or fear [Actor]
passage:
"Uma, come! Everyone's at the park gate!"
"For the trees?"
"They're cutting the banyan tomorrow. Listen to them!"
"SAVE OUR PARK! SAVE OUR PARK!"
"Tanuja, you're shouting louder than the uncles."
"I can't help it! My chest feels like it's on fire. Everyone's so angry."
"Are you angry?"
"I... yes? I mean, I love that tree."
"Look, the contractor's truck."
"Go away! Go away! Uma, give me your bottle."
"Why?"
"I'm going to throw it at the windscreen."
"Tanuja. You don't even throw paper at people."
"..."
"Hold the banner with me instead. We'll write to the ward office tonight."
"Okay. Okay. My hands are shaking. That wasn't even me just now."

qa.q: What was going to be cut tomorrow?
qa.a: The banyan.

qa.q: What did Tanuja mean by "That wasn't even me just now"?
qa.a: Tanuja realised the urge to throw the bottle came from the crowd's anger sweeping through, not from how Tanuja normally feels or acts.

qa.q: What turning point did Uma create, and why did it help?
qa.a: Uma reminded Tanuja "You don't even throw paper at people" and offered the banner and a letter instead, giving the strong feeling a safe outlet.

qa.q: How might Uma see Tanuja's shouting at the gate?
qa.a: Uma notices Tanuja is louder than the uncles, unusual behaviour that shows the crowd's energy has taken hold.

grounding: A teenager at a neighbourhood rally is swept up in the crowd's anger and nearly acts out of character, until a friend offers a steadier way to join in.
